title: Consumer Awareness
summary: ## Definitions
A consumer is a person who buys goods and services, or who uses them with the buyer's permission. A person who buys for resale is not a consumer.

Goods are products made and sold to consumers through wholesalers and retailers. Services include banking, insurance, transport, electricity, housing, water, health and entertainment, but not free services or personal-service contracts.
Consumer awareness is knowledge of four things:
(1) the quality of the product, including its effect on health and the environment;
(2) the hazards of marketing, such as misleading advertisements;
(3) consumer rights, including how to claim compensation;
(4) the consumer's own responsibilities, such as avoiding wasteful and unnecessary consumption.
## Need for consumer awareness
(1) The market is flooded with goods and sellers, so it is hard to know which are genuine; online and phone orders add distance between buyer and seller.
(2) Advertisements hide information.
(3) Expiry dates on food and medicines are often not shown or noticed.
(4) Goods are sold without a bill to avoid VAT, a tax charged whenever value is added. The government loses revenue, and the consumer has no proof of purchase if the product is faulty.
(5) Producers are organised into associations, while consumers are weak and unorganised.
(6) Consumers waste resources and do not dispose of waste safely.
## Laws

The Consumer Protection Act 1986 (CPA) is the most important law. It gives consumers support and guidance, and it provides cheap, simple and quick justice. It applies to all goods and services in the private, public and cooperative sectors, and it covers municipal services too. Other laws are the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954, the Essential Commodities Act 1955, and the Standard of Weights and Measures Act 1976.
## Institutions
Councils: the Central Consumer Protection Council, headed by the Union minister, and the State Consumer Protection Councils.
Consumer courts are quasi-judicial and have three tiers:
(1) District Consumer Forums — 604 in the country — for claims up to ₹20 lakh;
(2) State Commissions — 35 — for claims up to ₹1 crore;
(3) the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, for claims above ₹1 crore.
Relief should be given within 90–150 days. Appeals go to the next tier within 30 days.

NGOs file cases, give support and educate consumers. Examples are the Consumer Guidance Society of India, Common Cause, Consumer Grievance and Consumer Forum. Jago Grahak Jago is a government campaign.
## Filing a complaint

Keep the bill or cash memo. Use the prescribed format, choose the category (unfair trade practice or deficiency of service), describe the fault and the remedy wanted (replacement, refund or compensation), and attach the evidence. Make three copies and pay a nominal fee by demand draft.
File within 2 years of the defect. You may appear in person or through a representative, a lawyer or a letter; complaints can also be emailed. A frivolous complaint can be fined up to ₹10,000.
Grounds for complaint include deficiency of service — any fault or shortcoming in the quality or manner of the service — and defective goods.
## Consumer rights
(1) Right to information: price, weight, brand, manufacturing and expiry dates, ingredients and quality marks. Example: an air fare shown as ₹1,500 turned out to be ₹4,995 with taxes.
(2) Right to choose: not to be forced to buy extras, as when a gas agency made a buyer purchase a ₹7,000 'kit'.
(3) Right to safety: protection from goods dangerous to health and life, such as adulterated food or unsafe electrical goods.
(4) Right to be heard: consumers' interests receive due consideration, and they can voice complaints fearlessly.
(5) Right to seek redressal: compensation for unfair trade practices.
(6) Right to consumer education: access to information and to quality marks such as ISI, AGMARK and BIS.
## Consumer responsibilities
Do not be misled by advertisements; children are the worst victims of deceptive ads.
Buy quality-certified products: ISI on industrial and consumer goods, AGMARK on agricultural and food products. Check expiry dates.
Demand a bill.
Be a green consumer: use biodegradable products instead of plastic bags, save electricity and gas, and use public transport.
Act as managers, like Gujarat's 13,000 village Pani Samitis that run their own water supply.
## Concerns of the consumer movement
(1) Rural consumers are often illiterate and face fake brands, spurious goods, no warranties and unreasonable prices.
(2) Delays: justice delayed is justice denied. Cotton farmers took 14 years to win a case. The CPA was amended in 2003 to limit adjournments.
A successful consumer movement needs people to be aware and educated.

objective: State True or False: (a) The ISI mark certifies the quality of agricultural food products. (b) AGMARK certifies industrial consumer goods.

(a) False — ISI is for industrial and consumer goods.
(b) False — AGMARK is for agricultural and food products.
Fill in the blanks: (a) Consumers should not indulge in ______ consumption. (b) Consumers should avoid ______ consumption.
Give one word: (a) The bottom tier of consumer courts. (b) The top tier of consumer courts.

(a) District Consumer Forum.
(b) National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC).
Name the consumer right in each case: (a) A person falls sick after eating a packaged food. (b) A seller forces a buyer to buy one brand and shows no other.

(a) Right to safety.
(b) Right to choose.
Fill in the blanks: (a) A complaint must be filed within ______ years of the defect. (b) An appeal to a higher consumer court must be made within ______ days.
State True or False: (a) A consumer buys both goods and services. (b) The CPA covers only the private sector.

(a) True.
(b) False — it covers the private, public and cooperative sectors.
vsa: A green consumer buys and uses products that do not harm the environment — biodegradable goods instead of plastic bags — saves electricity and gas, and uses public transport or eco-friendly vehicles.
Explain the right to be heard.
It ensures consumers' interests receive due consideration in the right forums, and it empowers them to complain fearlessly against defective products and erring sellers.

Sellers must give full information — price, weight, brand, manufacturing and expiry dates, ingredients, quality marks and contact details — so consumers can make informed choices. Example: an air fare of ₹1,500 turned out to be ₹4,995 with hidden taxes.

or: Explain the right to consumer education.
Consumers have the right to programmes and information that help them decide before and after purchase — government and NGO guidelines and awareness of marks such as ISI, AGMARK and BIS.

vsa: The market is flooded with goods and sellers, advertisements mislead, expiry dates and bills are often skipped, and consumers are unorganised. So they must know their rights to avoid being cheated, and their duties to avoid waste.
A consumer is a person who buys goods or services, or uses them with the buyer's permission. A person who buys goods for resale is not a consumer.
Why is a bill important when buying goods and services?
The bill is proof of purchase, needed to return a faulty product or file a complaint in a consumer court. It also ensures the seller pays tax (VAT) to the government.
Consumers have the right to protection against goods and services that are dangerous to health and life, such as adulterated food, spurious medicines and unsafe electrical goods.
sa: 'Children are the worst victims of deceptive advertisements.' Explain.

Advertisements use attractive audio-visuals, show only eye-catching parts and hide crucial information.
Children cannot judge such claims and easily want junk food, toys and gadgets they see on TV.
So parents must guide them and teach them not to be misled.
Explain the need for consumer awareness in rural India.

Rising incomes have expanded rural markets, and companies now sell there.
But rural consumers are often illiterate and ignorant of their rights.
They face fake brands, spurious goods, no warranties, imitations and unreasonable prices.
Awareness helps them demand bills, check quality marks and expiry dates, and seek redressal.
Explain the right to safety and the right to be heard.

Right to safety: protection against goods dangerous to health and life — adulterated food, spurious medicines, faulty electrical goods.
Right to be heard: consumers' interests receive due consideration in proper forums, and they can voice complaints fearlessly against erring sellers.
What problems may you face if you buy a geyser at a lower price without taking the bill?

(1) If the geyser is defective, you cannot get it repaired under warranty, replaced or refunded, since there is no proof of purchase.
(2) You cannot file a complaint in a consumer court.
(3) You help the seller evade VAT, so the government loses revenue.
(4) It may even be a spurious or unsafe product.
What are the grounds for filing a consumer complaint?

(1) Defective goods.
(2) Deficiency of service — any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality or manner of a service.
(3) Unfair or restrictive trade practices.
(4) Overcharging or short weight.
(5) Goods hazardous to life and safety.
la: Describe the procedure for filing a consumer complaint.

(1) Keep the bill, cash memo or receipt as proof of purchase.
(2) Write the complaint in the prescribed format (from the CPA booklet), choosing the category — unfair trade practice or deficiency of service.
(3) State the fault clearly and the remedy wanted: replacement, refund or compensation.
(4) Attach the evidence and make three copies — for yourself, the other party and the court.
(5) File before the right court by value (District up to ₹20 lakh, State up to ₹1 crore, National above), and pay a nominal fee by demand draft.
(6) File within 2 years of the defect, in person or through a representative, a lawyer or a letter, or by email. Appeal within 30 days.

or: Explain the role of NGOs in consumer protection.

When the seller ignores a complaint, NGOs such as the Consumer Guidance Society of India, Common Cause, Consumer Grievance and Consumer Forum help.
(1) They help consumers file cases in consumer courts.
(2) They provide logistic, manpower and legal support.
(3) They run programmes to educate consumers about their rights and responsibilities.
(4) They test products and publicise unfair practices. The government's Jago Grahak Jago campaign also spreads awareness.

la: Explain the consumer redressal system in India.

Laws: the Consumer Protection Act 1986 is the most important law, giving cheap, simple and quick justice for all goods and services. Others are PFA 1954, ECA 1955 and SWMA 1976.
Councils: the Central Consumer Protection Council (headed by the Union minister) and State Councils.
Consumer courts (quasi-judicial, three tiers): District Consumer Forums (604, up to ₹20 lakh), State Commissions (35, up to ₹1 crore), and the National Commission (above ₹1 crore). Relief should come within 90–150 days, with appeals to the higher tier.
NGOs also help consumers file cases.
What kinds of knowledge are needed for consumer awareness?

(1) Knowledge of the product's quality — whether it is good for health and safe for the environment.
(2) Education about the hazards of marketing — misleading advertisements must be verified.
(3) Knowledge of consumer rights — to get the right product and to claim compensation under the law if it is faulty.
(4) Knowledge of the consumer's own responsibilities — no wasteful or unnecessary consumption, demanding a bill, being a green consumer.
How does the Consumer Protection Act 1986 provide support and guidance to consumers?

(1) It gives cheap, simple and quick justice, with less paperwork and less delay.
(2) It applies to all goods and services in the private, public and cooperative sectors, including municipal services.
(3) It sets up three-tier consumer courts and protection councils.
(4) Consumers can choose where to seek redressal, and a company cannot insist on its own court.
(5) It covers real estate developers and foreign e-commerce sellers, and it guarantees rights to information, choice, safety, being heard, redressal and education.
